sections.heading: Honoring you as the Maker and ruler of everything
sections.text:
King of glory, you are greater than we can take in. Everything good, pure, wise, and strong belongs to you. Heaven and earth are yours; the whole world and everything in it belongs to you.

You made all things from nothing, and you still hold all things together. You rule over nations, homes, and every individual life. Nothing is too large for your power, and nothing is too small for your care.
theological_themes: God is glorious, perfect, and worthy of worship.
God created all things and owns all things.
God rules wisely over the whole world and over ordinary personal lives.

scripture_references.connection: This psalm grounds worship in the truth that the earth and all who live in it belong to the Lord because he founded it. That supports the prayer’s confession that all creation is God’s possession.
Paul presents God as the Creator who gives life to all and appoints the times and places of nations. This fits the prayer’s movement from God’s cosmic rule to his care over nations and individuals.

sections.heading: Recognizing that every creature depends on you
sections.text:
Your goodness has no edge or limit. Every living thing depends on you for breath, food, strength, and help. We do not keep ourselves alive; we receive life from your hand.

Your mercy is precious to us. Your faithful love is better than anything we could build, buy, or chase. Draw our hearts toward you again.
theological_themes: All creatures depend on God’s provision.
God’s goodness and mercy are abundant.
God’s lovingkindness draws people to himself.

scripture_references.connection: The psalm describes all creatures looking to God and being fed by his open hand. It directly supports the prayer’s confession that every creature is supplied by God.
This passage praises the preciousness of God’s steadfast love and pictures people finding refuge and life in him. It illuminates the prayer’s delight in God’s mercy and goodness.

sections.heading: Asking to find our happiness in you, not in lifeless things
sections.text:
Teach us to put our deepest happiness in you, the blessed God. Keep us from trying to find real life in things that cannot give it. Do not let us spend ourselves asking for what only fools us for a while and leaves us empty.

Let your favor matter more to us than comfort, success, or praise. Give us again the joy of being saved by you. Let us learn to say, honestly and gladly, that our true home, treasure, and heaven are found in you.
theological_themes: God himself is the believer’s highest joy and satisfaction.
Earthly things cannot give the life and fullness only God gives.
The joy of salvation is a gift to be sought from God.

scripture_references.connection: David speaks of fullness of joy and lasting pleasure in God’s presence. This supports the prayer’s request to find its deepest happiness in God himself.
God rebukes his people for leaving him, the fountain of living waters, for broken cisterns. That gives biblical weight to the prayer’s warning against seeking life in dead and empty things.
David asks God to restore the joy of salvation after confessing sin. This fits the prayer’s request that God would give renewed joy in his saving mercy.

sections.heading: Thanking you for caring for us through Christ
sections.text:
Father, you have cared for our happiness better than we ever could. We are fallen people, and yet you have not abandoned us. In love and pity, you gave us a Savior.

Apply the redemption of Jesus to us deeply and truly. Declare us right with you because of him, not because of anything in us. And change us from the inside out, so that our desires, habits, and character become more like his.
theological_themes: God’s love provides a Savior for fallen sinners.
Christ’s redemption must be personally applied to believers.
Justification and sanctification are distinct gifts of salvation in Christ.

scripture_references.connection: This passage connects God’s goodness and loving kindness with salvation through Christ, justification by grace, and renewal by the Holy Spirit. It closely matches the prayer’s request for redemption applied in both standing and inward change.
Paul explains that sinners are justified by God’s grace through the redemption in Christ Jesus. This supports the prayer’s plea to be justified through Christ rather than by our own merit.
Christ gave himself not only to redeem people from lawlessness but also to purify them for a life of good works. That supports the prayer’s request for sanctified natures, not only pardoned guilt.

sections.heading: Bringing our need and weakness to you
sections.text:
We confess our sins to you. Have mercy on us.

We are tired; give us rest. We are ignorant; make us wise for salvation. We are helpless; let your strength show itself in our weakness. We are poor and needy; give us the riches that are ours in Christ.

When we are confused, tempted, and afraid, keep us moving forward with you. Do not let us be stopped by discouragement or shaken by fear. Help us remember what you have promised: you will never leave us or forsake us.
theological_themes: Confession of sin and dependence on God’s mercy.
Christ gives rest to the weary and wisdom to the needy.
God’s strength is displayed in human weakness.
God’s presence sustains believers through confusion and temptation.

scripture_references.connection: John teaches believers to confess sins to God, trusting him to forgive and cleanse. This grounds the prayer’s honest confession and plea for mercy.
Jesus invites the weary and burdened to come to him for rest. This directly supports the prayer’s request for rest from the Lord.
Paul says the Scriptures are able to make a person wise for salvation through faith in Christ Jesus. This fits the prayer’s request that God make the ignorant wise in the way of salvation.
Christ tells Paul that divine power is made perfect in weakness. That supports the prayer’s request that God’s strength be displayed precisely where we are helpless.
This passage applies God’s promise never to leave or forsake his people as the basis for courage and trust. It directly grounds the prayer’s closing confidence in God’s faithful presence.

sections.heading: Ending with praise
sections.text: Blessed be your name. You are enough for us, and all our hope is in you. Amen.
theological_themes: Praise is the fitting response to God’s sufficiency, mercy, and saving care.
The believer’s hope rests in God himself.

scripture_references.connection: The psalm calls the soul to bless the Lord for forgiveness, healing, redemption, steadfast love, and renewal. It reflects the prayer’s final turn from need to praise.

content_provenance.original_author: Unattributed Puritan source (compiled and edited by Arthur Bennett)
content_provenance.original_source: The Valley of Vision: A Collection of Puritan Prayers and Devotions, ed. Arthur Bennett (The Banner of Truth Trust)
content_provenance.source_copyright_status: Compilation, titles and arrangement in copyright (Banner of Truth, 1975); underlying Puritan sources are public domain.
content_provenance.modern_version_note: Contemporary prayer based on the theological themes and ideas of the historical source; not a reproduction of the original wording.

significant_interpretive_choices: The original phrase “never seeking life among the dead things of earth” was rendered as seeking real life in things that cannot give it, preserving the concrete contrast between God as living source and earthly substitutes without implying that creation itself is evil.
“Find our heaven in thee” was interpreted as finding ultimate joy, treasure, and home in God now, rather than making a claim about the full doctrine of the afterlife.

“Apply his redemption to our hearts, by justifying our persons, and sanctifying our natures” was kept as both justification and sanctification, preserving the Puritan distinction between our legal standing before God and God’s inward work of holiness.
